tix.title: Check a business
tix.subtitle: Before extending credit, a contract, equipment or postpaid service — find out what other participating institutions have reported.
tix.advisoryNotice: This is an indicator requiring review, not a finding of misconduct.
tix.purposeHint: Recorded on the audit trail. Every search has to be able to answer 'why did you look this up'.
tix.forbidden: Your account does not have permission to run verifications.
tix.networkError: Could not reach the verification service.

declare.title: Declare a default
declare.subtitle: Report a subscriber who has defaulted, so other operators can see the status before extending credit. Only the status crosses the exchange — never the amount.
declare.fullNameHint: As held on your own records. Used for matching, and never shown to another operator.
declare.identifierHint: Separators and case are ignored. RCCM or tax number identifies a business most reliably.
declare.amountHint: Must be at or above the reporting threshold, which is 100 USD.
declare.currencyHint: A currency with no configured threshold is refused rather than assumed.
declare.defaultDateHint: Not the date you are reporting it. The retention clock runs from this date.
declare.dunning: I confirm the contractual dunning process ran before this declaration, and the subscriber was given the opportunity to pay.
declare.subjectCreatedBody: The exchange had no record of this subject before now. They are in the registry because of this declaration.
declare.subjectExisted: This subject was already known to the exchange. Your record has been added to what is held about them.
declare.retentionNote: The record is erased automatically on the retention date. Settling it brings that date forward and can never push it back.

records.title: My records
records.subtitle: Everything your organisation has declared. Other operators see only the status of these records — never the amount, the service, or your name.
records.settleNote: Marking a record settled brings its erasure date forward and stops it counting against the subject. Marking it disputed suspends it from inquiry results while the dispute is open.

tix.checkDescription: Identify the company by its register number where you can. Names are unreliable: operator exports truncate them, and different companies share them.
tix.identifierTypeHint: Optional if you have the exact registered name.
tix.legalNameHint: As registered. On its own this resolves a business when exactly one in the registry carries that exact name — a personal name is never enough by itself, because names collide.
tix.whatIsNotShown: The exchange never tells you the amount, the service, or which institution reported it. You are told that an obligation exists and its status — the rest is the other operator's commercial information, and the same rule protects yours.

outcomeExplained.NO_MATCH: No participating institution has reported this identifier.
outcomeExplained.CLEAR: Known to the exchange, with nothing outstanding against them.
outcomeExplained.OUTSTANDING_DEBT: At least one institution reports an unpaid obligation.
outcomeExplained.REVIEW_REQUIRED: The identifier matched, but not confidently enough to act on. Check by hand.

tix.accountReferenceNote: Only this organisation can match on it. Account numbers are assigned by each operator from one upwards, so the same number belongs to a different company at every operator — records identified this way stay visible to you and invisible to the exchange. Map an RCCM or tax number as well when the file has one.

hero.title: A trusted national intelligence platform for better business decisions.
hero.body: Search businesses or individuals, understand financial exposure, identify risk signals, detect fraud, and make faster decisions from one secure intelligence network designed for institutions across the Democratic Republic of Congo.
checks: Every inquiry logged with its purpose

board.title: Universal Intelligence Search
board.signal: Driven by obligations over a year overdue, reported by more than one participating institution. The total owed is weighed in four wide bands, never disclosed as a figure.

platform.title: From fragmented records to a trusted national intelligence layer.
platform.body: DIP is designed to become a nationally trusted infrastructure where approved institutions can securely contribute, validate, and consult risk intelligence while retaining ownership of their operational data.

cards.title: Universal Entity Search
cards.body: Search businesses and individuals across available participating data sources using names, identifiers, phone numbers, account references, and other approved attributes.

cards.title: Identity Resolution
cards.body: Match inconsistent names, aliases, identifiers, phone numbers, and historical records to create a trusted entity profile with confidence scoring.

cards.title: Risk Intelligence
cards.body: Combine payment behaviour, aging, exposure, disputes, source history, and fraud indicators into transparent risk insights for human decision makers.

cards.title: Fraud and Anomaly Detection
cards.body: Surface duplicate identities, unusual relationships, repeated defaults, conflicting information, suspicious account patterns, and potential data-quality problems.

exchange.title: From spreadsheet to shared intelligence network.
exchange.body: Start with secure file ingestion today. Evolve toward real-time APIs and multi-institution intelligence as participating organizations connect.

steps.title: Ingest
steps.body: Excel, CSV, secure uploads, APIs, and scheduled feeds.

steps.title: Validate
steps.body: Schema checks, missing values, formats, reconciliation, and source quality.

steps.title: Resolve
steps.body: Normalize names, detect duplicates, match entities, and assign confidence.

steps.title: Enrich
steps.body: Exposure, aging, history, relationships, fraud indicators, and trends.

steps.title: Decide
steps.body: Search, risk reports, alerts, APIs, dashboards, and human review.

boundary.title: Institutions share a verdict, not their books.
boundary.body: The reason a competing operator will join is not what the exchange reveals. It is what it refuses to.
received: Whether an adverse record exists, and its status
How confident the identity match is
withheld: Account references, tariffs, usage, or any operational data
Anything at all about a record while it is under dispute
boundary.note: Enforced by the database, not by the application. A participant's rows are unreadable to another participant's connection; the exchange relaxes reads for one specific question and never relaxes writes.
boundary.purpose: Every inquiry is rate-limited and recorded with a stated purpose. Each one is individually legitimate — the aggregate is what turns a lookup service into a bulk export.

risk.title: A risk profile built from evidence, not a black box.
risk.body: The DIP Risk Indicator is a sum of stated factors, each published with its weight. It is an indicator rather than a credit score, and it says so: 0 is no adverse information and 100 is the most the platform can observe.
risk.notAssessedNote: Two factors are deliberately never weighed, and the reason for each is printed beside the assessment: disputes, which are already withheld from every answer the exchange gives, and fraud indicators, whose signal the registry's own uniqueness rules make impossible. Outstanding exposure joined them until August 2026, when counsel confirmed the operator files are in US dollars; it is now weighed in four bands wide enough that no sequence of readings recovers the amount.

entity.title: Business and individual intelligence in the same platform.
entity.body: Different users need different evidence. DIP maintains separate profiles, permissions, signals, and reporting for businesses and individuals.

cards.title: Business Intelligence
cards.body: Search organizations, consolidate operator records, review payment exposure, aging, account status, identifiers, business relationships, and risk indicators.

cards.title: Individual Intelligence
cards.body: Resolve identities using approved personal identifiers and historical records, surface payment and fraud signals, and support responsible onboarding decisions.

cards.title: Portfolio Monitoring
cards.body: Monitor existing customers and portfolios for new debt, aging changes, fraud indicators, write-offs, disputes, and material risk changes.

trust.title: Designed to become a trusted reference across institutions.
trust.body: DIP is not another isolated database. Its long-term role is to provide a governed national intelligence network that banks, telecom operators, insurers, utilities, enterprises, and authorized public institutions can rely on when assessing identity, exposure, and risk.

cards.title: Verified Institutional Data
cards.body: Intelligence is derived from approved participating sources, with provenance retained for every record.

cards.title: Shared Rules, Clear Ownership
cards.body: Participants retain ownership of their operational data while DIP applies governed sharing and access rules.

cards.title: Every Search Accountable
cards.body: Searches, reports, exports, and risk reviews are designed to be logged and auditable.

cards.title: Built to Grow Nationwide
cards.body: The architecture supports growth from initial telecom datasets to a broader multi-industry national intelligence ecosystem.

industries.title: One platform. Different decisions.
industries.body: DIP serves as the shared intelligence foundation while each industry receives workflows and risk views tailored to its own operating model.

cards.title: Banking and Lending
cards.body: Customer due diligence, business search, identity matching, pre-credit risk indicators, portfolio monitoring, fraud signals, and API-based decision support.

cards.title: Telecom Intelligence Exchange
cards.body: Shared telecom debt intelligence, aging exposure, customer hopping indicators, account history, duplicate records, and onboarding risk support.

cards.title: Insurance
cards.body: Identity verification, business due diligence, anomaly indicators, customer relationships, and configurable underwriting support signals.

cards.title: Utilities and ISPs
cards.body: Assess service applicants, monitor unpaid balances, identify repeat defaults, and share approved risk information across participating networks.

cards.title: Enterprise Trade Risk
cards.body: Search companies before offering credit, contracts, equipment, postpaid services, or supplier terms. Monitor strategic counterparties continuously.

cards.title: Public Sector
cards.body: Use governed identity, business, and risk intelligence for authorized public-sector verification, licensing, collections, and program-integrity workflows.

portfolio.title: Understand exposure before it becomes a loss.
portfolio.body: Dashboards help decision makers see concentrations, aging, operator exposure, high-risk entities, recovery priorities, and data quality across the portfolio.

ai.title: Ask questions across the intelligence network.
ai.body: Analysts get an evidence pack: exactly the facts they are already entitled to, assembled in one place with the provenance of each and an explicit list of what is not there and why. No language model is configured in this deployment — the grounding was built first, because an analyst with direct database access would answer questions this exchange spends its whole design refusing. Final lending, onboarding, fraud and service decisions remain with authorized humans.

exchanges.question: Why is this business classified as moderate risk?
exchanges.answer: The primary drivers are aged outstanding telecom balances and repeated late-payment indicators. Identity confidence is high and no material fraud indicators are currently present. Review the detailed exposure timeline before extending additional terms.

exchanges.question: Show me companies with high exposure and aging above 180 days.
exchanges.answer: I found 14 entities matching the selected portfolio criteria. The largest exposure concentration is within enterprise telecom accounts. Open the filtered portfolio view to review source records and recovery status.

subjects.title: A national registry is only defensible if the people in it can answer back.
subjects.body: A shared bad-payer list decides who can open a line, take a loan, or win a contract. That is real power over people who did not choose to be in it, and the rights below are built rather than promised.

cards.title: Ask what is held
cards.body: A person can obtain their whole file across every participating institution — not only the one whose office they happened to walk into.

cards.title: Dispute, and be suppressed while it is examined
cards.body: A contested record stops being reported to other institutions the day the dispute is raised. Before the decision, not after: the harm of being wrongly listed accrues every day the listing stands.

cards.title: Be forgotten on a clock
cards.body: Every record carries an expiry set from the date the obligation fell due, never from the date it was reported — so reporting a debt late cannot keep somebody listed for longer. When it passes, the record is deleted rather than hidden.

cards.title: Not be added by asking
cards.body: Looking somebody up never creates them. Somebody who comes forward to ask whether they are listed does not become listed by asking.

subjects.note: Retention periods are configuration, not constants, because they are legal periods. The values in the current build are the terms of reference's illustrative figures and are being checked against the Code du numérique before anyone should treat them as settled.

governance.title: Intelligence without surrendering control.
governance.body: Each participating institution retains ownership of its operational data. DIP controls access through permissions, audit trails, purpose-based workflows, tenant isolation, and configurable information-sharing rules.

cards.title: Role-Based Access
cards.body: Users see only the data and actions permitted for their organization and function.

cards.title: Complete Traceability
cards.body: Every search, report, update, export, and risk review can be logged and investigated.

cards.title: Data Minimization
cards.body: Share the intelligence required for a decision without unnecessarily exposing underlying operational data.

cards.title: Decision Support
cards.body: DIP provides risk evidence and recommendations; authorized institutions retain final decision authority.

status.title: What runs today, and what comes next.
status.body: Much of this page describes a design. This section says which parts of it exist, because a platform asking institutions to trust it with a national dataset should be the kind that tells them.
built: Bilingual platform, sign-in, roles, and tenant isolation enforced by the database
Declaring a default, with a reporting threshold below which nothing enters the registry
Cross-operator inquiry returning status only, rate-limited and audited with a stated purpose
How many institutions report a subject — never which, never how much, never since when
CSV and Excel import with immutable raw storage and provenance for every row
Turning imported rows into records, through a mapping the operator defines and versions
Importing a delivery keyed on the operator's own account numbers, or on nothing but a name
Taking a published delivery back, and taking back every record derived from it
The DIP Risk Indicator, with every factor and weight published beside the figure
Searching your own book by name or identifier
Retention, expiry, and erasure that deletes rather than hides
Subject access, dispute, withdrawal, and erasure requests, on statutory deadlines
An operator exposure view, aged, per currency
designed: The identity resolution queue: candidate matches reviewed and decided by a person
Consolidated entity profiles for businesses and individuals
open: The currency of the amount column in the operator deliveries, which nothing in either file states
Whether a written-off debt is a status or a different kind of record
Whether the reporting threshold survives contact with real data
What lawful basis under article 192 the exchange operates on
status.note: The columns below are the honest state of the platform. Figures shown elsewhere on this page illustrate the product rather than report a live national registry.

finalCta.title: Turn the data you already have into intelligence you can act on.
finalCta.body: Start with existing telecom spreadsheets. Add new institutions, APIs, and risk capabilities as the network grows.

footer.tagline: Dival Intelligence Platform (DIP) · Telecom Intelligence Exchange (TIX)

notifications.subtitle: Alerts and reminders addressed to you

messages.debtDeclared: A debt of {amount} was declared against {subject}
messages.orgUnitCreated: {name} was added to the organization structure
messages.probationEnding: Probation for {employee} ends in {days} day(s) with no decision recorded
messages.reviewAssigned: You have a review to write for {employee} in {cycle}
messages.reviewBothSubmitted: Both assessments are in for {employee} in {cycle}
messages.reviewShared: Your {cycle} review has been shared with you
messages.tixInquiryResultSuperseded: A record you were told about has been corrected or withdrawn. Check subject {subject} again before relying on the earlier answer.
messages.watchedSubjectChanged: {name}: the exchange now says {outcome}, with {institutions} institution(s) reporting.

imports.title: Data imports
imports.subtitle: Deliver a file, look at what was stored, then publish it or send it back. Nothing is derived from a delivery until it is published.
imports.sourcesDescription: Successive deliveries of the same export share one source, so their history is one history.
imports.noSources: No sources yet. Register one before uploading.
imports.newSourceCodeHint: Short and stable, e.g. VODACOM_POSTPAID. Case and spacing are normalised.
imports.uploadDescription: The file is sent as-is and parsed on the server, so the checksum and the stored rows describe the same bytes.
imports.fileHint: CSV or XLSX. A header that sits below blank rows or an unlabelled total is found; quoted fields, commas inside names and Windows line endings are handled. Dates in a spreadsheet arrive as Excel serial numbers, and the old binary .xls is not supported.
imports.batchesDescription: Every file this organisation has sent, whatever became of it.
imports.batchSubtitle: The rows exactly as stored. Nothing here has been interpreted.
imports.checksum: SHA-256 of the file as received
imports.checksumHint: Compare this against your own copy to confirm the platform holds the file you sent.
imports.rowsDescription: The first 50 rows, as they were delivered. These cannot be edited — only replaced by a new delivery.
imports.profileDescription: Counted over every row, and nothing here decides what any column means. Which one is a balance and which is an identifier is still an open question; how many cells are filled is not.
imports.profileNote: A column whose distinct count equals its filled count is unique on every row, which is what an identifier looks like. A column with one distinct value is a constant and carries no information. Values are shown only where there are few enough of them to be a vocabulary rather than a customer list.
imports.issuesDescription: Problems that hold whatever the columns turn out to mean. Nothing is rejected — every row is stored exactly as delivered — but these will not survive the mapping, and it is cheaper to fix the export than to explain the gap later.
imports.issuesNone: Nothing structurally wrong with this delivery.
imports.issuesMissingIdentifierNote: Blank in a column that is unique everywhere else
imports.issuesTruncated: Only the first rows are listed. The counts above are complete.
imports.asAtHint: The date these balances were true. Asked rather than guessed: the export carries no dates, and every record derived from it starts its retention clock here.
imports.mappingDescription: Your answer, not ours. The profile above says which columns are unique, which are constant and which are entirely numeric — DIP cannot tell which of ten numeric columns is the balance, and will not guess.
imports.mappingNone: No mapping defined for this source yet. Nothing can be derived until there is one.
imports.mappingIdentifierHint: The one unique on every row. In the profiled export that is the account reference.
imports.mappingAmountHint: The balance owed. Aging buckets are numeric too, and they are not it.
imports.mappingCurrencyHint: Fixed for this source. The file does not say.
imports.mappingProfileNote: Optional. Sector, city and street are what let a reviewer tell two companies of one name apart from one company that re-registered — the case a changed RCCM creates. Neither current delivery carries them; a file prepared against the published template does.
imports.mappingReplaceNote: Saving does not edit the current mapping — it supersedes it. Deliveries already derived keep the rules they were derived under.
imports.deriveDescription: Separate from publishing on purpose. Publishing accepts the delivery; this makes the people in it visible to every other operator on the exchange.
imports.deriveDunning: I confirm the contractual dunning process ran for these accounts
imports.deriveDunningHint: A typed declaration carries this per record. An import has to carry it too, and it is recorded against you.
imports.deriveTruncated: Only the first refusals are listed. The counts above are complete.
imports.mappingNoIdentifier: This file has no identifier column
imports.mappingNoIdentifierNote: This delivery identifies nobody by number, so the name column identifies the subject. It works only inside your own organisation — another operator asking about the same company finds nothing, because nothing in the file says it is the same company. If two rows carry the same name the whole delivery is refused, since importing both would record two companies as one.
imports.rowsFailed: The stored rows could not be loaded.
imports.mappingFailed: The mapping for this source could not be loaded.

participants.title: Participating organisations
participants.subtitle: Every institution on the exchange, what kind it is, and whether it is currently contributing and consulting.
participants.listDescription: An exchange is only worth what its participants contribute. This is who they are.
participants.suspendNote: Suspending an organisation stops it declaring and inquiring. Its existing records stay, and stay visible — withdrawing a participant is not a reason to rewrite what other operators already relied on.
participants.addDescription: Creates the tenant. Signing the data-sharing agreement happens outside this screen.
participants.name: Legal name
participants.slugHint: Lower case, hyphenated. Appears in URLs and cannot be changed afterwards.
participants.sectorHint: Decides which industry edition the organisation sees.
participants.onboardingNote: Per DATA_GOVERNANCE.md, a source is not accepted until the sharing agreement, permitted-use definition, retention rules and a pilot import are all in place. This screen creates the account, not the permission.
participants.needPlatformAdmin: This view belongs to whoever runs the network. Sign in as a platform administrator to see it.

portfolio.title: Exposure
portfolio.subtitle: What your organisation is owed, aged from the date each obligation fell due. Counted from your own records only — never another operator's.
portfolio.recordsNote: Excludes anything past its retention date
portfolio.awaitingErasureNote: Past retention and not yet purged. This should be back to zero every morning.
portfolio.exposureDescription: Never combined into one total. Adding 500 USD to 500 CDF gives a number that is not of anything, and it looks entirely normal on a dashboard.
portfolio.agingDescription: Measured from the date the obligation fell due, not the date it was reported. Settled debts are not aged — otherwise a portfolio would look older the more of it you had recovered.
portfolio.agingFootnote: The bands match the columns of the telecom exports we receive. The boundary above 270 days is ours: the source files label their last column “360 +” with nothing between, so where a 300-day debt belongs has not been confirmed with the operator.
portfolio.statusDescription: Disputed and investigated records are withheld from other operators, but they are still money you are owed.
portfolio.serviceDescription: As submitted by whoever declared the record.
portfolio.provenanceDeclared: Declared through the API or this application
portfolio.provenanceNote: Records derived from an uploaded file, counted separately from those declared through the API. Both are real records held to the same rules; the distinction is provenance, so an auditor asking where a figure came from gets an answer on the screen.
portfolio.empty: Your organisation has not declared anything yet, so there is nothing to age.
portfolio.noAccess: Your account can make inquiries but not declare records, so there is no portfolio to show.

subjectRights.title: Subject requests
subjectRights.subtitle: Cases raised by the people in the registry. Every one has a statutory deadline.
subjectRights.overdueNote: Past the period the Code du numérique allows
subjectRights.queueDescription: Oldest first. A case is overdue when the statutory period has run out and it is still open.
subjectRights.noAccess: Your account cannot see subject requests. The declarant role opens cases; the compliance officer role decides them.

typeHints.ACCESS: Tell me what you hold about me. Sixty days, article 210.
typeHints.RECTIFICATION: This is wrong. Thirty days, and the records are suppressed meanwhile.
typeHints.ERASURE: Remove it. Thirty days. Granted for settled records, refused with reasons for outstanding ones.
typeHints.DISPUTE: I do not accept this debt. Thirty days, and the records are suppressed meanwhile.

subjectRights.raiseDescription: The person has to already be in the registry. Looking somebody up here never creates them.
subjectRights.raiseDetailHint: What the person actually said. Optional, and worth recording.
subjectRights.notInRegistry: Nobody in the registry holds that identifier. That is the answer they came for, and it is not an error.
subjectRights.verifyDescription: Nothing can be decided or disclosed until this is done. "I am that person" is otherwise enough to erase somebody else's debts.
subjectRights.verifyEvidenceHint: Free text and mandatory. "National ID CD-1234-5678 seen in person, photograph matches" is something a regulator can assess; a ticked box is not.
subjectRights.discloseDescription: Everything the exchange holds about this person, across every operator. The one call that crosses the boundary on the subject's behalf, and the most heavily audited read in the system.
subjectRights.discloseEmpty: No operator holds a record against this person.
subjectRights.erasureDescription: Settled records are erased; outstanding ones are kept, with written grounds. An unconditional right would let anybody delete their own debts, and no operator would contribute to an exchange that worked that way.
subjectRights.decideDescription: Upholding leaves the records suppressed and tells every institution that was given the old answer. Refusing puts them back into the exchange.
subjectRights.decideReasonHint: The person has to be able to challenge this, and they cannot challenge silence.
subjectRights.cannotDecide: Deciding cases needs the compliance officer role. Whoever takes a request at the counter should not also rule on it.
subjectRights.select: Select a case to work on it.
subjectRights.withdrawTitle: The person is no longer pursuing this
subjectRights.withdrawDescription: Closes the case without deciding it, and puts back anything it suppressed. Available until a decision is made.
subjectRights.withdrawNoteHint: Something a regulator could check — "Called on 14 May, said she had settled directly with the shop". A case closed with no decision and no record of who asked is indistinguishable from one quietly dropped.

search.title: Search
search.subtitle: Find a business or a person in your own book. What other operators hold is a separate question, asked through an inquiry.
search.scopeNote: This searches records your organisation declared. A subject can be reported by several operators — finding one here means you hold a record against them, and finding nothing here does not mean nobody does.
search.placeholder: Trading name, RCCM, tax number, phone number…
search.noResults: Nothing in your book matches that.
search.noResultsHint: To find out whether another operator holds a record, run an inquiry instead.
search.noAccess: Your account can make inquiries but has no book of its own to search.
search.profileSubtitle: Everything your organisation holds about this subject.
search.notHeld: You hold no record against this subject.
search.identifiersDescription: As the exchange stores them, normalised. Matching runs on this form, so if a search for what is printed on a document fails, the difference is visible here.
search.recordsDescription: Your own records only. Aged from the date each obligation fell due.
search.inquire: Ask the exchange about this subject

audit.title: Audit trail
audit.subtitle: What your organisation's accounts have done, newest first. Every inquiry carries the purpose it was made for.
audit.noAccess: Reading the trail needs the auditor, compliance officer or tenant administrator role. An account cannot be the only reader of its own record.
audit.inquiriesNote: Each one carries a stated purpose
audit.refusalsNote: Denied attempts are kept, not discarded
audit.eventsDescription: The most recent are shown. Counts above are over the whole trail.
audit.actorNote: Accounts are shown by identifier rather than by name. The trail belongs to no single part of the platform, so it deliberately does not depend on the part that knows people's names.
audit.immutableNote: Rows are appended and never changed. A correction is a further event, never an edit — which is why a refused attempt is still here.

risk.title: DIP Risk Indicator
risk.scaleNote: 0 is no adverse information. 100 is the most this platform can observe. This is an indicator, not a credit score.
risk.whyTwo: {band} is driven primarily by {first} and by {second}.
risk.whyNothing: Nothing adverse is reported against this subject by any participating institution.

drivers.DEBT_AGING: how long the oldest unpaid obligation has been overdue
drivers.REPORTING_INSTITUTIONS: more than one participating institution reporting an unpaid obligation
drivers.IDENTITY_CONFIDENCE: a match resting on a name and nothing else
drivers.FRAUD_INDICATORS: one identifier appearing under more than one subject

notAssessedReasons.MIXED_CURRENCY: The amounts on this subject's file are not all in one currency, and adding them would mean inventing an exchange rate. Exposure is left unweighed rather than part-added, because a total smaller than the real one is the error that costs a lender money.
notAssessedReasons.DISPUTES_ARE_NOT_DISCLOSED: A record under dispute is already withheld from every answer the exchange gives, before anybody decides who is right. Reporting the dispute itself would restore that disclosure by another route and make contesting a record something that costs the person who contests it.
notAssessedReasons.NO_FRAUD_SIGNAL_IS_COMPUTABLE: The signal this factor rested on — one identifier held by two different subjects — cannot occur: both unique indexes on the identifier table forbid it, which is exactly how a business register number resolves to one company. So the factor reported Low on every assessment ever made, which is the most reassuring possible way to report having looked at nothing.

risk.modelNote: Assessed under model {version}. Every factor and its weight is published above; nothing here is a black box.
risk.noIndicator: No assessment: the exchange did not confirm a match, so there is nothing to assess.

settings.title: Settings
settings.subtitle: What this deployment is configured to do, and where each value came from.
settings.readOnly: Read-only. Shortening a retention period would put records past due the moment it was saved, so changing these is a decision with an audit entry behind it rather than a text box on a page.

groups.rights: Answering the people in the registry

groupNotes.retention: These are legal periods rather than engineering constants. Two were the terms of reference's illustrative figures until counsel answered in August 2026; the third was never asked about and is still unchecked, which is what the labels on the right are for.
groupNotes.rights: How long there is to answer somebody asking about their own record. Shortened sharply in August 2026 — access was sixty days and everything else thirty. A case keeps the deadline it was given when it was raised, so this binds new requests rather than making yesterday's queue overdue.
groupNotes.reporting: A currency absent from this list is refused rather than defaulted, so the row that is missing is itself a setting. CDF is deliberately unset: choosing it means choosing a USD/CDF rate that moves and that somebody has to own.
groupNotes.exchange: The exchange holds competitors' records and every request is individually legitimate. The limit does not make a bulk sweep impossible; it makes it slow enough for the audit trail to be read.
groupNotes.models: Compiled into a release rather than configured, and shown because a threshold you cannot see is a threshold you have to take on trust.

keys.RETENTION_REPEAT_YEARS: A default by somebody who has defaulted before
keys.RETENTION_SETTLED_DAYS: A debt survives this long after it is settled
keys.MINIMUM_DECLARABLE: Nothing below this enters the registry
keys.INQUIRIES_PER_HOUR: Inquiries one institution may make in an hour
keys.MATCH_REVIEW_THRESHOLD: Confidence at which a candidate pair reaches a reviewer
keys.MATCH_STRONG_CONFIDENCE: Confidence above which a reviewer will probably agree
keys.RIGHTS_ACCESS_DAYS: To supply a copy of what is held
keys.RIGHTS_OTHER_DAYS: To answer a rectification, erasure or dispute

provenanceNote.UNVERIFIED_PLACEHOLDER: A plausible figure nobody has checked against the law. It will hold until somebody decides it, and it should not be quoted as though somebody had.
provenanceNote.NOT_SET: Nothing is configured, so this is refused rather than defaulted.
provenanceNote.LEGAL_ADVICE: A lawyer was asked this question and answered it in August 2026. That is the strongest footing anything on this page has, and it is still not a regulator's approval.

access.title: Access and permissions
access.subtitle: Who holds which role here, and what holding it actually permits.
access.loadFailed: Could not load access and permissions.
access.derivedNote: This list is read from the guards the application enforces, every time the page loads. It is not a description maintained alongside the code, so it cannot drift from it.
access.readOnlyNote: Read-only. Roles are held in the identity provider; granting one there is where the decision is recorded.
access.rolesDescription: Counted in endpoints, grouped by the part of the product they belong to.
access.membersDescription: Roles as recorded when each person last signed in.
access.noMembers: Seeing who is in your organisation needs the tenant administrator role.
access.grantsNothing: Grants nothing. This role can be assigned and will change nothing for the person who receives it.
access.authenticatedNote: Not a role. Endpoints open to every signed-in account, each one a deliberate decision, listed so the catalogue does not silently omit them.

resolution.title: Identity Resolution Center
resolution.subtitle: Records that may be the same person or company, for somebody to decide.
resolution.why: The DRC has no single identifier covering everybody, so two institutions reporting one person create two records and nothing in either file says they are one. Resolving that is the registry's work, not a participant's: the pair below is one operator's record beside another's, and neither of them may see it.
resolution.loadFailed: Could not load the review queue.
resolution.scanResult: Compared {compared} pair(s) across {subjects} subject(s); opened {opened} case(s).
resolution.emptyHint: Either the registry holds no pair alike enough to be worth a person's time, or somebody has already been through them.
resolution.unavailableNote: Three signals are never held: no delivery carries a second phone number, a city or an address. They are listed rather than omitted, because a reviewer who reads nothing there would conclude the records disagreed — and because those three fields would move a decision further than any refinement of the name comparison could.
resolution.neutralNote: Two institutions number their own customers from one upwards, so every genuine cross-operator match has different customer numbers. Shown because a reviewer will notice it; weighted at nothing because reading it as evidence would refuse all of them.
resolution.notePlaceholder: The national ID on both operators' KYC files is the same.
resolution.noteHint: Required on every outcome. The merge can be undone; the reason somebody believed two records were one person cannot be recovered from anywhere else.
resolution.confirmWarning: Confirming moves both institutions' records onto one subject. The absorbed record is kept, pointing at the survivor, so this can be traced and undone.
resolution.modelNote: Compared under model {version}. Every signal and its weight is published above.
resolution.forbidden: This queue belongs to the registry. Each case shows one institution's record beside another's, with both names — so a participant holding it would be reading a competitor's customer file, which is the disclosure the exchange exists to prevent. Sign in as a platform administrator to review. Participants receive the result as a better match, never as the queue.
resolution.whoYouAre: Signed in as {name}, holding: {roles}. If PLATFORM_ADMIN is not in that list, this session is not a registry account — and if it is, the refusal came from the API rather than from this page, which is a different problem.
resolution.registerNumberNote: A register number that differs weighs much less against a match than one that agrees weighs for it. An RCCM is reissued when a company amends its statutes or adds capital, so two different numbers may be two companies or one company before and after a change — and nothing in either file says which. A conflicting tax number still settles it.

directory.businessesSubtitle: Companies your institution has reported, in name order.
directory.individualsSubtitle: People your institution has reported, in name order.
directory.ownBookNote: Your own book only. An institution can browse the people it has itself reported and nobody else's — the difference between a directory of your records and a directory of the country.
directory.forbidden: Browsing the book needs the declarant role. An account that may only enquire submits an identifier and receives a verdict, rather than a list.
directory.emptyBusinesses: You have not reported any company, or every record has passed its retention date and been erased.
directory.emptyIndividuals: You have not reported any individual. Both real operator deliveries are business portfolios, so this stays empty until somebody sends a subscriber file — and a subscriber file with a date of birth is what would make identity resolution work for people.
directory.truncated: Showing the first {count}. Narrow it with search rather than scrolling.

anomalies.title: Fraud and anomalies
anomalies.subtitle: How your own people have been using the exchange.
anomalies.why: Everything else in DIP checks whether a record is right. This checks whether the asking is right — the one question an institution cannot answer for itself, and the reason every inquiry has been recorded with its actor, its outcome and a stated purpose since the rate limiter went in. Nothing had ever read those rows back.
anomalies.notAccusation: None of these is an accusation. Every one has an innocent explanation that is usually the true one: a collections team working a list, an integration retrying, somebody new mistyping. The figures are here so you can ask.
anomalies.cannotDetect: What this cannot tell you, and will not pretend to: one identifier under two customers, one phone on two accounts, one document under two names. The registry's uniqueness rules make all three impossible, which is how a business register number resolves to one company. An alert that can never fire is a permanently green light, and a permanently green light is worse than none.
anomalies.forbidden: Reading how colleagues have used the exchange is a supervisory function. It needs the compliance officer or tenant administrator role.
anomalies.empty: Nobody at your institution has used the exchange in the last {days} days.
anomalies.windowNote: Last {days} days. Compared against your institution's own median of {median} inquiries per person — a relative measure, because a call centre and a two-person office have nothing in common and any fixed number would be wrong for both.
anomalies.nothingUnusual: Nothing unusual. Everybody's figures are shown so the absence of a flag means somebody looked, rather than that nothing was checked.

flagNotes.HIGH_VOLUME: More than four times the institution's median, and above the floor below which one busy afternoon is not a pattern.
flagNotes.MOSTLY_NO_MATCH: The strongest of the three and the hardest to explain away. Somebody checking customers finds them; somebody walking an identifier format to see which values exist finds almost nobody.
flagNotes.HIT_THE_RATE_LIMIT: A person doing their job reaches an hourly cap approximately never. Something automated reaches it immediately.

watchlist.title: Watchlists
watchlist.subtitle: Companies you are asking the exchange about on a schedule.
watchlist.why: A watch is not a new power. It is the inquiry you can already make, asked every night, charged against the same hourly allowance and recorded in the same audit trail with the same stated purpose. It reports exactly what an inquiry would have reported that morning: an outcome and how many institutions report the company — never which.
watchlist.whyNightly: Answered on a schedule rather than the moment something happens, and that is deliberate. Being told the afternoon a rival declares would tell you when, and when plus a count of two identifies the other institution by elimination.
watchlist.forbidden: Watching a company needs the inquirer role, because a watch is an inquiry.
watchlist.emptyHint: Open a company from Businesses or from a search result and start a watch there. You will be asked why, as you are for any inquiry.
watchlist.sweep: Ask about all of them now
watchlist.sweepResult: Asked about {watched}; {changed} answer(s) changed. That cost {watched} inquiries against this hour's allowance.
watchlist.expiryNote: A watch stops after twelve months. Somebody who still needs it renews it and says why again — a list that only ever grows is surveillance by accretion.

executive.title: Executive intelligence
executive.subtitle: As at {date}. Every figure is a count of rows somebody can open and check.
executive.nothingVisible: Your account carries none of the roles these figures belong to. Nothing is hidden from you here that you would be able to act on.
executive.bookNote: Records this institution has declared, as they stand now. Not a history: the platform snapshots nothing, so there is no honest figure for what this looked like last quarter.
executive.bookContestedNote: Withheld from every answer the exchange gives while the case is open.
executive.activityNote: Counted from the audit trail and from when each record entered the registry. This is the only history the platform holds, which is why it counts events rather than balances.
executive.activityScale: All three series share one scale. The tallest bar is {peak}.
executive.activityEmpty: Nothing recorded in the last thirteen months.
executive.rightsTitle: Answering the people in the registry
executive.rightsNote: Every request ever raised against this institution, measured against the deadline that request carried — not the one in force today. The periods shortened in August 2026, and judging older cases by the newer rule would invent a failure that never happened.
executive.rightsLateNote: Article 214 makes a missed deadline grounds in itself for a complaint.
executive.rightsNothingAnswered: Nothing has been decided yet, so there is nothing here to be early or late.
executive.absences: Two figures are deliberately absent. There is no chart of exposure over time, because nothing snapshots what was owed on a past date and drawing one would mean assuming records existed continuously from their default date — an assumption dressed as history. And there is no count of how many inquiries came back with a debt, because the audit trail records that a question was asked and what it was for, never what it returned. Recording the answer would keep a second copy of the disclosure under the audit period rather than the retention period, and turn the trail into a searchable shadow of the exchange.

analyst.title: Dival AI analyst
analyst.subtitle: Everything the platform can honestly say about one company, and what it cannot.

ask.title: Ask DIP
ask.note: The model reads your question; the platform computes the answer. Every figure below is counted from records you are already entitled to see — no number here was written by a language model.
ask.placeholder: Which businesses owe us more than 20,000?
ask.unsupported: That is not one of the questions this analyst can answer. It is a short list on purpose: the analyst chooses from it rather than writing its own query, so a misread question produces the wrong answer to a question of yours rather than reaching data you may not see. Try one of the suggestions above.
suggestions: Which businesses owe us more than 20,000?
Which businesses owe more than 20,000 across multiple institutions?
What changed in our portfolio this week?
Which accounts should our collection team prioritise?

intents.EXPOSURE_ABOVE: Understood as: companies owing you above a threshold
intents.EXPOSURE_ABOVE_MULTI_INSTITUTION: Understood as: the same, reported by more than one institution
intents.WHY_RISKY: Understood as: why one company looks risky
intents.WHAT_CHANGED: Understood as: what changed in your book
intents.PRIORITISE: Understood as: which accounts to work first

ask.readByRules: question read by the built-in rules
ask.writtenBy: Sentence phrased by {model} from the figures above. The figures were computed before it was written and do not depend on it.
ask.yourExposureNote: "Your exposure" means what these companies owe you. DIP never discloses what another institution is owed, so no figure here is a market total — and one presented as such would be wrong.
ask.inquiryCost: Screening these {count} companies across institutions would cost {count} of your hourly inquiries, because how many institutions report a company is exactly what an inquiry discloses. Nothing has been spent: this is a quote.

caveats.NO_MODEL_PRODUCED_THIS: No language model wrote any of this. None is configured in this deployment; the boundary was built before the model rather than after.
caveats.OTHER_OPERATORS_ARE_NOT_NAMED: How many institutions report, never which. A count is a fact about the company; a name is a fact about a competitor's customer relationship.
caveats.OTHER_OPERATORS_AMOUNTS_ARE_NOT_DISCLOSE: What another institution is owed is not here. Yours is, in full. An amount from elsewhere would tell you the size of a rival's commercial relationship, which is not a fact about the debtor.
caveats.CONTESTED_RECORDS_ARE_WITHHELD: A contested record leaves the exchange the moment it is contested — and not only the record of the institution it was raised against. Every record about that company is withheld, including yours, before anybody decides who is right. So the exchange can answer "clear" with nought institutions while live debts are still on file. Silence here is emphatically not absence of debt. Your own file above is unaffected: suppression governs what the exchange tells others, not what you may see of your own.
caveats.NO_NATIONAL_DOCUMENT_IS_HELD: This company has no register number, tax number or other national document on file — nothing that identifies it to anybody but you. That is the concrete thing to go and collect.
caveats.THE_EXCHANGE_WOULD_NOT_CONFIRM_IDENTITY: The match fell below the threshold at which the platform will answer without a person looking, so anything it might have said is withheld rather than guessed. Not a finding about the company.

ask.noCompany: No company of that name is in your book. The name was taken from your question, so this is as likely to be a misread as a missing company — try the company's registered name.
